title: Two-Step Sign-In
about: Add a second lock to your accounts so a password alone isn't enough.

cards.prompt: A stranger far away has your password. What else can they grab?

items.label: A password stolen in a website hack
Your pet's name, which you posted online

cards.explanation: Anything you know or type can be copied and used from anywhere. Your phone and fingerprint stay with you.
cards.hint: Can it be copied from afar, or is it physically with you?
cards.nudge: Information copies from far away; things in your pocket or body can't.

cards.sentence: **Two-step sign-in** asks for your password **plus** a second proof, like a code on your phone.

cards.prompt: A sign-in code arrives when someone types your password.

steps.text: Your phone buzzes: **"Your sign-in code is 481 902."** You didn't sign in. What does it mean?

choices.text: Someone has my password and is trying to sign in
choices.consequence: Right. The code stopped them, but they know your password.
Codes arrive when someone tries to sign in. Someone did, and it wasn't you.

steps.text: A friend messages: **"Oops, I sent you my code! Send it back?"**

choices.consequence: That was the attacker. The code was for your account, and now they're in.

choices.text: Don't send it. Change your password
choices.consequence: Good. Change your password, and warn your friend another way.

cards.explanation: A code you didn't ask for means someone has your password: change it. Never send a code to anyone.
cards.hint: Codes arrive when someone tries to sign in; nobody real asks for one.

cards.sentence: A **passkey** signs you in with your face, fingerprint or PIN: the strongest, since fake sites can't use it.
An **authenticator app** makes fresh codes on your phone, safer than codes sent by text.

cards.prompt: Strongest to weakest: drag them into order.
cards.explanation: A passkey is strongest, then an app code, then a text code. A password alone is weakest.
cards.hint: Which proofs could a scammer far away steal, and which can't they?
cards.nudge: Any second proof beats a password alone. Which can scammers sometimes steal?

cards.prompt: A password manager keeps a different strong password for every account.

choices.text: A password manager, locked with two-step
choices.consequence: Right. Every account gets its own strong password, and two-step guards the manager.
One password everywhere has the same flaw: one breach opens all 40.

choices.text: An easy pattern: game1, game2, game3
choices.consequence: A pattern is quick to guess, and one leak reveals the rest.

cards.explanation: A password manager gives each account its own long password, and fills it only on the real site.
cards.hint: What happens to the other 39 if one password leaks?

cards.prompt: A music app only offers text codes for two-step.

steps.text: Text codes are the weakest. Turn it on?

choices.text: Yes: a weak lock beats no lock
choices.consequence: Right. Anyone with just your password is now stuck without the code.

choices.text: No: text codes can be stolen
choices.consequence: Stealing a phone number is hard work. Most attackers have only a password, and a text code stops them.
That could take years. Until then your account has only one lock, so turn on what's offered.

cards.explanation: Any second proof beats none. Turn on the best one a site offers, and switch if a better one comes.
cards.hint: Which is harder to break into: a password plus a text code, or a password alone?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **Two-step sign-in** adds a second proof, so a stolen password isn't enough.
- **Never share a sign-in code.** Got one you didn't ask for? Change your password.
- **Try this:** turn on two-step sign-in for one account, with an adult.

**Next:** the email that pretends to be someone you trust.
